Ex vivo studies in brain slices further showed that cannabinoids reduce inhibitory input from neighboring neurons, releasing a “brake” on SOM activity.

title: Joint processing of arrow direction and number magnitude strengthens Spatial-Numerical Associations: evidence from a modified flanker task
Understanding Understanding: Reconnecting Theories of Human Semantic Knowledge
abstract: At the close of the twentieth century, human semantic memory was thought to be organized around dedicated, domain-specific modules operating independently of one another and of perception, action, and much of language. The intervening years have marked a transition toward a more holistic view in which semantics emerges from learned mappings among sensory, motor, and language representations, with recent work beginning to integrate semantic representation with theories of cognitive control and attention. This article reviews the reasons for this remarkable change in perspective, provides a snapshot of our current understanding of semantics in the mind and brain, and considers how this understanding may change in light of new innovations in artificial intelligence.

title: How we study what we study: A methodological review of 50 years of educational technology research
abstract: Research in educational technology has been extensively mapped in terms of what has been studied, but far less attention has been paid to how it has been studied. This paper reports a methodological review of fifty years of research in Computers & Education, covering a corpus of 5,516 articles published between 1976 and 2026, with the principal findings based on the post-1996 full-text corpus. Using an AI-assisted analysis, applied to full texts and abstracts, we traced the evolution of research paradigms, approaches, and methods across the journal's full publication history. The principal findings are based on the post-1996 full-text corpus. Pre-1996, full-text machine-readable files were not available for analysis. Analysis of pre-1996 abstracts was possible and are included to provide context for trends observed post-1996. The findings show that quantitative approaches and questionnaire-based data collection have constituted the field's sustained methodological centre of gravity. Within this dominant pattern, two shifts stand out: 1) the rise of systematic reviews as a recognised approach, and 2) a computational turn. The range of methods used in research has grown steadily, suggesting a gradual broadening of the field's repertoire. These patterns are only visible across multiple decades. Findings reveal that quantitative dominance is not a recent development but a persistent structural feature, and that the computational surge is better understood as a second wave following a peak in the mid-2000s. These findings have implications for what kinds of knowledge educational technology research is equipped to produce. The study argues that understanding a field's methodological history is a prerequisite for extending it.

title: Relations between Teachers’ and Students’ Social-emotional Competence: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-analysis
abstract: Abstract Social-emotional competence (SEC) is strongly associated with key educational outcomes, including students’ academic achievement, engagement, and well-being as well as teachers’ effectiveness and occupational well-being. Although evidence for the extent and conditions of association between teachers’ and students’ SEC has accumulated for over two decades, the pattern among relations remains largely unexplored. This systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis followed PRISMA guidelines and searched four databases (PsycINFO, ERIC, Scopus, Web of Science). We identified 65 studies and 196 effect sizes ( N = 23,409 teachers; N = 241,233 students) for examination of the relationship between teachers’ and students’ SEC. Results demonstrated a moderate overall correlation between teachers’ and students’ SEC, although the magnitude of this association varied considerably across studies. We found moderating effects for students’ socioeconomic status (SES), teachers’ years of experience, method by which SEC were measured, and grade levels. The positive association between teachers’ SEC and students’ SEC persisted across sensitivity analyses. However, funnel plot asymmetry and the Egger test indicated that publication bias could not be ruled out, hence the magnitude of the pooled estimate should be interpreted with caution. When the multidimensional construct of SEC was examined across five separate domains (see CASEL, 2020), teachers’ responsible decision-making showed the largest observed relationship with overall students’ SEC, while students’ relationship skills showed the strongest observed association with overall teachers’ SEC. However, given substantial heterogeneity and uneven numbers of effect sizes across SEC domains, these relative differences should be interpreted with caution. Overall, the findings indicate an association between teachers’ and students’ SEC, while also highlighting considerable variability in the magnitude of this relationship. These findings also suggest that teachers’ SEC merits closer attention in social-emotional research with students, including studies designed to test whether teachers’ SEC yields benefit for students’ own SEC development.

title: “How do we overcome this?” expansive potential of community collaboration in urban development
A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity
abstract: Abstract While most contemporary motivation research has approached sociocultural and individual processes separately, any person’s experience, motivation, and action are simultaneously sociocultural and individual. In this article, we propose the Complex Dynamic Systems (CDS) paradigm as a framework for integrating sociocultural and individual processes into a coherent account of motivated action, and we elaborate one CDS model—the Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity (DSMRI; Kaplan & Garner, 2017). Our central argument is that the DSMRI explains motivated action as an emergent phenomenon grounded in the person’s role identity—a complex dynamic system that itself emerges within a culturally mediated activity system. This yields an integrated, two-level explanation of the foundational motivational question, why does this person act this way in this situation? At the first, sociocultural level, a person acts according to the sociocultural role they occupy in a particular cultural activity system; at the second, individual level, different people occupying the same role construct idiosyncratic role identities that are framed by the role, yet emerge uniquely because they manifest as non-deterministic dynamic systems. In the article, we develop the conception of culture in the DSMRI as a complex, dynamic, symbolically mediated cultural activity system, and the role identity system that emerges within it. We conclude by considering the implications of this conception for motivation theory, research, and the design of educational environments.

title: How young children learn mental state words: Decision processes and links to theory of mind
abstract: Learning words that refer to mental states is a critical developmental milestone, yet how these words are learned remains poorly understood. In this study, 102 Chinese young children (Mage = 3.28; 45 girls) and 102 young adults (Mage = 22.67; 54 women) completed a novel word-learning task, in which a pseudoword was paired with videos depicting goal-directed reaching and distressed crying. Results indicated that children had difficulty learning mental state words, as reflected by their lower accuracy compared to adults. Diffusion model analyses further explored the underlying processes and found that children's difficulties did not reflect deficits in perceptual encoding of behavioral information or response execution. Instead, children accumulated evidence more slowly and adopted more conservative decision thresholds when inferring underlying mental states. Moreover, better theory-of-mind ability in children was associated with narrower decision thresholds, indicating that children with stronger social cognitive abilities required less evidence to learn mental-state meanings. Overall, these findings offer insights into the mechanisms underlying mental state word learning and advance our understanding of the complex interaction between children's social cognition and language development.

title: Young children can infer what speakers know based on their causal influence over listeners
Examining associations between monitoring-related parenting phenotypes and youth externalizing using a discordant sibling random-intercept cross-lagged panel model
abstract: In this registered report, we introduce a new discordant sibling random-intercept cross-lagged panel model and apply it to investigate within-person/family and between-family bidirectional associations of parental monitoring-related phenotypes and youth externalizing behaviors. We used data from 1,956 twin/sibling pairs (Mage at first assessment = 10 years; 51% male, 59% White; 14% Black; 15% Hispanic; <1% Asian; 11% Other race/ethnicity) contributing up to six annual waves of data collection from the adolescent brain and cognitive development study, a nationally representative data collection effort including 11,875 children enrolled and assessed across 21 sites across the United States. DS latent curve models with structured residuals models were needed to account for change over time, converged, and fit the data well. We found few within-person/family effects consistent with hypotheses, concentrated from age 13-15 that were likely environmentally mediated. Potentially causal effects within-person/family effects included more youth-reported child disclosure at age 13 predicting lower parent-reported externalizing at age 14, and more youth externalizing problems at age 13 with less monitoring at age 14; other within-person/family associations were driven by familial confounding. Unexpected positive between-family lagged effects in the same developmental window reflect novel family-level processes that may be driven by evocative gene-environment correlations.
